items.prompt: When the brake pads rub on a bicycle wheel, the force that slows the bicycle is called ___.
hints: Think about what happens when two surfaces rub together.
This force always acts against the direction something is moving.
Rub your hands together quickly. The force you feel starts with the letter f.
items.explanation: Friction acts between surfaces that rub together. The brake pads rub on the wheel, and friction slows the bicycle down.

items.prompt: Sort these into useful friction and unhelpful friction.

items.text: a heavy box that is hard to slide

hints: Friction is useful when we want grip or want to slow something down.
Friction is unhelpful when it wears things out, makes a noise or makes moving harder.
Start with the shoes. Think about walking on a floor with no friction at all.
items.explanation: Friction helps shoes grip, brakes stop, pencils leave marks and matches light. It is unhelpful when it wears out chains and tyres, makes hinges squeak or makes boxes hard to slide.

items.prompt: Why does a parachute fall slowly?

options.text: It has no weight.
options.why: A parachute has weight, so gravity still pulls it down.

options.text: Gravity does not pull on parachutes.
options.why: Gravity pulls on everything that has mass, including parachutes.

options.text: It is made of plastic, which floats on air.
options.why: Plastic does not float on air. The large shape is what slows it.

options.text: Its large surface pushes against lots of air, making big air resistance.

hints: Air pushes against anything that moves through it.
Think about how the size of a surface changes how much air it pushes against.
Compare an open parachute with a closed one. Decide which falls more slowly.
items.explanation: A parachute has a large surface, so it pushes against a lot of air as it falls. This makes a large air resistance force, which slows the fall.

items.prompt: Which shape moves most easily through water?

options.text: a smooth, pointed shape like a fish
a flat, wide square
options.why: A flat, wide shape pushes against lots of water, so it is slowed down.

options.text: a rough box with sharp corners
options.why: Rough surfaces and sharp corners make more water resistance.

options.text: an open umbrella shape
options.why: An open umbrella catches lots of water, so it is slowed down a lot.

hints: Water pushes against things that move through it. This is water resistance.
Think about the shape of fast swimmers such as fish and dolphins.
Look for the shape with the smallest front and the smoothest sides.
items.explanation: A smooth, pointed shape is streamlined, so water flows around it easily. Fish, dolphins and boats have streamlined shapes to reduce water resistance.

items.prompt: Sinta pulls the same shoe across four surfaces with a forcemeter. Which conclusion fits her results?

figure.alt: Bar chart of the force needed to pull a shoe: tiles 2 N, wood 3 N, carpet 5 N and sandpaper 7 N.

options.text: Smoother surfaces give more friction.
options.why: The smooth tiles needed the smallest force, so they gave the least friction.

options.text: All surfaces give the same friction.
options.why: The forces are different for each surface, from 2 N to 7 N.

options.text: Rougher surfaces give more friction.
The shoe is heavier on carpet.
options.why: The same shoe was used each time, so its weight did not change.

hints: A bigger force to pull the shoe means more friction.
Put the surfaces in order from smoothest to roughest.
Compare the bar for tiles with the bar for sandpaper.
items.explanation: The smooth tiles needed only 2 N and rough sandpaper needed 7 N. Rougher surfaces give more friction, so a bigger force is needed to pull the shoe.

items.prompt: Choose all the ways to reduce friction.

options.text: put oil on a squeaky hinge
make the surfaces smoother
put a heavy box on rollers
spread sand on a slippery path
options.why: Sand makes the path rougher, which increases friction so people can grip.

options.text: wear shoes with deep rubber grooves
options.why: Deep grooves give more grip, which means more friction.

hints: Friction is greater when surfaces are rough and pressed together.
Think about how a squeaky bicycle chain can be made to stop squeaking.
For each choice, ask whether the surfaces will grip more or slide more easily.
items.explanation: Oil, smooth surfaces and rollers all let surfaces move past each other more easily, so they reduce friction. Sand and deep grooves increase friction to give more grip.

items.prompt: In 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon at the same time. They hit the ground together. Why?

options.text: The Moon has no gravity.
options.why: Both objects fell, so the Moon's gravity was pulling on them.

options.text: There is no air on the Moon, so there is no air resistance.
The hammer and the feather have the same mass.
options.why: The hammer has much more mass than the feather.

options.text: The feather is heavier on the Moon.
options.why: Everything weighs less on the Moon, including the feather.

hints: On Earth, a feather falls slowly because air pushes against it.
Think about what is all around us on Earth but missing on the Moon.
Take the air out of the problem. Decide what would then slow the feather down.
items.explanation: On Earth, air resistance slows a feather much more than a hammer. The Moon has no air, so there is no air resistance, and gravity makes both fall at the same rate.

items.prompt: Hana drops a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled ball of the same paper from the same height. Which lands first, and why?

options.text: The flat sheet, because it is heavier.
options.why: Both are made from the same sheet of paper, so they have the same mass.

options.text: They land together, because they have the same mass.
options.why: In air, shape changes the air resistance, so the flat sheet is slowed more.

options.text: The crumpled ball, because its smaller surface meets less air resistance.
The flat sheet, because air pushes it down.
options.why: Air resistance pushes against the movement, so it slows the flat sheet.

hints: Both pieces have the same mass, so gravity pulls on them equally.
Think about which shape pushes against more air as it falls.
Picture each one falling. Decide which has the bigger surface facing the air.
items.explanation: The ball and the sheet have the same mass, but the flat sheet has a much bigger surface. It meets more air resistance, so the crumpled ball lands first.

items.prompt: Four parachutes made of the same material carry the same toy. Order them from the slowest fall to the fastest fall.
hints: A falling parachute is slowed by air resistance.
A bigger surface pushes against more air.
Decide whether a wide or a narrow parachute meets more air resistance, then sort them by width.
items.explanation: The wider the parachute, the more air it pushes against and the bigger the air resistance. So the 100 cm parachute falls most slowly and the 10 cm parachute falls fastest.

items.prompt: A skydiver jumps from a plane. At first she speeds up, but later she falls at a steady speed. Why does she stop speeding up?

options.text: Gravity switches off high in the sky.
options.why: Gravity keeps pulling on her all the way down.

options.text: Her mass gets smaller as she falls.
options.why: Her mass does not change during the fall.

options.text: Air resistance becomes zero.
options.why: Air resistance is biggest when she falls fast. It does not become zero while she moves.

options.text: Air resistance grows as she speeds up, until it balances her weight.

hints: Two forces act on her: her weight pulling down and air resistance pushing up.
Air resistance gets bigger the faster you move.
Ask what happens when the upward force grows until it matches the downward force.
items.explanation: As she falls faster, air resistance grows. When it becomes as big as her weight, the forces are balanced, so she stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed.

items.prompt: Rani drags a box to the right across a rough floor. Label the three forces on the box.

figure.alt: A box rests on the floor. A long arrow points right from the box. A shorter arrow points left along the floor from the box. Another arrow points straight down from the middle of the box.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
Friction acts against the way the box moves.
Weight is the pull of gravity, so it acts downwards.
items.explanation: Rani pulls to the right. Friction pushes back against the movement, and weight pulls the box down.

items.prompt: Label the parachute. The up arrow shows the force of the air on the canopy. The down arrow shows the pull of gravity.

figure.alt: A parachute with a curved canopy at the top, three strings meeting at a block hanging below. An arrow beside the parachute points up and another points down.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The upward force slows the fall, and it comes from the air.
The downward arrow is the pull of gravity on the load.
items.explanation: The canopy catches air. Air resistance pushes up and weight pulls down. A big canopy means more air resistance.

items.prompt: Tap the shoe sole that will grip best on a wet floor.

figure.alt: Four shoe soles. Top left: a smooth sole. Top right: a sole with three shallow lines. Bottom left: a sole with many deep grooves. Bottom right: a sole with two shallow lines.

hints: Grip comes from friction between the sole and the floor.
Water makes floors slippery, so the water must be able to escape.
Look for the sole that has the most deep channels.
items.explanation: Deep grooves push water out of the way, so more of the sole touches the floor. This gives more friction.

items.prompt: The three shapes are pushed through water from left to right. Tap the shape that has the least water resistance.

figure.alt: Three solid shapes of similar size are held in water that flows from the left. A is a tall rectangle with a flat front. B is a triangle with a flat front facing the flow. C is a long diamond with a pointed front.

hints: A streamlined shape lets water slip past it.
Water resistance is large where a flat face pushes against the water.
Look for the shape with a pointed front and a narrow body.
items.explanation: A pointed, narrow shape pushes less water out of the way, so it has less water resistance.

items.prompt: Bayu rolls a toy car down a ramp onto four surfaces. Work out the mean distance for each surface and complete the table.
head: Surface
Trial 1 (cm)
Trial 2 (cm)
Mean (cm)
hints: The mean is the middle value of two readings added together.
Add the two trials, then divide by 2.
Carpet: 52 + 56 = 108. Now halve it.

items.prompt: Bayu tests ice next. Using the table, which result is most likely?

head: Surface
Mean distance (cm)
figure.alt: Table of mean distances a toy car rolled: sandpaper 32 cm, carpet 54 cm, wood 90 cm, glass 128 cm.

options.text: Less than 32 cm, because ice is cold.
options.why: Cold does not stop a car. Friction decides how far it rolls.

options.text: More than 128 cm, because ice has even less friction than glass.
About 54 cm, because ice is a solid.
options.why: Wood and glass are solids too, and they gave very different distances.

options.text: The same as glass, because both are smooth.
options.why: Ice is usually even smoother and gives less friction.

hints: Look at the pattern: smoother surfaces give longer rolls.
Friction is least on the smoothest surfaces.
Is ice smoother or rougher than glass?
items.explanation: The smoother the surface, the less friction and the further the car rolls. Ice is very smooth, so it should roll furthest.

items.prompt: Wira drops parachutes of different widths from the same height with the same load. Which conclusion fits the bar chart?

figure.alt: Bar chart of fall time for parachutes with canopy widths: 10 cm falls for 2 seconds, 20 cm for 4 seconds, 30 cm for 5 seconds and 40 cm for 7 seconds.

options.text: The wider the canopy, the longer the parachute takes to fall.
The wider the canopy, the faster the parachute falls.
options.why: The wider canopies have longer bars, so they took more time and fell more slowly.

options.text: The width of the canopy makes no difference.
options.why: The bars get taller as the width grows, so width matters.

options.text: Heavier loads fall for longer.
options.why: The load was kept the same in this test, so we cannot say.

hints: Read the fall time for each width.
A longer fall time means a slower fall.
Compare the 10 cm bar with the 40 cm bar.
items.explanation: Wide canopies catch more air and have more air resistance, so they fall more slowly and take longer.

items.prompt: Use the bar chart. How many seconds longer did the 40 cm parachute take to land than the 10 cm parachute?

figure.alt: Bar chart of fall time for parachutes with canopy widths: 10 cm falls for 2 seconds, 20 cm for 4 seconds, 30 cm for 5 seconds and 40 cm for 7 seconds.

hints: Read the two bars.
Subtract the smaller time from the larger time.
The 40 cm bar is at 7 seconds.
items.explanation: 7 s - 2 s = 5 s longer.

items.prompt: Tom pulls a sled across snow with a forcemeter. The sled moves at a steady speed and the reading is 15 N. How big is the friction force on the sled?
hints: Steady speed means the forces are balanced.
The friction force must cancel the pull.
The two forces are equal in size.
items.explanation: At a steady speed the pull and the friction are balanced, so the friction is also 15 N.

items.prompt: The force of water pushing against a boat as it moves forward is called water ___.
hints: Think about the force that slows the boat down.
A similar force from air is called air resistance.
It starts with the letter r.
items.explanation: Water resistance is the force that water exerts against anything moving through it.

items.prompt: Order these surfaces from the most friction to the least friction.
hints: Rough surfaces grip more.
Water on a smooth surface makes it very slippery.
Sandpaper is the roughest on the list.
items.explanation: Rougher surfaces have more friction. Wet ice has the least.

items.prompt: Match each design to the reason for it.
pairs: Smooth shape of a bullet train
hints: Decide if the design adds or reduces friction.
Oil makes surfaces slide past each other.
Think about what moves through air.
items.explanation: Spikes and brake pads use friction. Oil and a smooth shape reduce friction and air resistance.

items.prompt: Sort each example by the kind of force that slows things down.
hints: Ask what the moving object is touching.
Air is a gas that moves around things.
Water resistance acts on things that move through water.
items.explanation: Two solids rubbing cause friction. Moving through air gives air resistance, and moving through water gives water resistance.

items.prompt: A heavy book rests on a sloping board and does not slide down. What is stopping it?

options.text: Nothing, because there is no friction when something is not moving.
options.why: Friction can act on things that are still. It stops the book from starting to slide.

options.text: Air resistance pushing the book up the slope
options.why: Air resistance only acts when something moves through the air.

options.text: The mass of the book is too small
options.why: A bigger mass would still be held by friction up to a point.

options.text: Friction between the book and the board

hints: The book wants to slide down because of gravity.
Something must act up the slope.
Which force acts between two touching surfaces?
items.explanation: Friction acts between the book and the board and stops it from sliding. Friction can act even when nothing moves.

items.prompt: Ines rubs her hands together quickly and they get warm. Why?

options.text: Her hands make heat from nothing.
options.why: Heat does not appear from nothing. It comes from the movement.

options.text: Air resistance cools her hands, then warms them.
options.why: Air resistance is not the main reason here.

options.text: Friction between her hands changes movement energy into heat.
Gravity pulls her hands together.
options.why: Gravity does not warm hands.

hints: Rubbing causes a force between surfaces.
This force also makes heat.
Brakes get hot for the same reason.
items.explanation: Friction between moving surfaces makes them warm. This is also why brakes get hot.

items.prompt: Choose all the changes that would help a toy boat move faster through water.

options.text: Make the front of the hull pointed.
Make the hull smoother.
Add a flat board at the front.
options.why: A flat board pushes against the water and slows the boat.

options.text: Make the boat wider and blunter.
options.why: A wide blunt shape has more water resistance.

options.text: Sand the bottom so it is less rough.

hints: You want less water resistance.
Smooth and pointed shapes slip through water more easily.
Cross out ideas that push against more water.
items.explanation: A pointed, smooth hull has less resistance, so the boat moves faster.

items.prompt: Hadi tests how far a car rolls on four floor types. He also uses a steeper ramp for the wood floor. What is wrong with this test?

options.text: He used four floor types, but should use two.
options.why: You can test many surfaces. The problem is something else that changed.

options.text: The height of the ramp changed, so it is not a fair test.
He measured distance, and should measure time.
options.why: Distance is a good measurement for this question.

options.text: Nothing, because a steeper ramp is better for wood.
options.why: Only the surface should change.

hints: Only one thing should change in a fair test.
Read what Hadi changed other than the floor.
Which variable should be kept the same?
items.explanation: Only the surface should change. A steeper ramp gives the car a faster start, so the results cannot be compared.

items.prompt: Putri cycles at a steady speed. She then crouches low over the handlebars and pedals just as hard. What happens?

options.text: She speeds up, because crouching reduces air resistance.
She slows down, because crouching makes her heavier.
options.why: Crouching does not change her mass.

options.text: Nothing changes, because pedalling is the same.
options.why: The air resistance changes with her shape.

options.text: She stops, because the friction in the tyres rises.
options.why: Crouching does not change the friction in the tyres much.

hints: What force pushes against a cyclist as she moves forward?
A smaller shape meets less air.
Her pedalling force stays the same.
items.explanation: Crouching makes her smaller, so less air pushes against her. With less air resistance, she speeds up.

items.prompt: A space capsule returning to Earth gets extremely hot and needs a heat shield. What causes the heat?

options.text: The cold of space heating the metal.
options.why: Space is cold. It does not heat the capsule.

options.text: Gravity squeezing the capsule.
options.why: Gravity pulls but does not make heat like this.

options.text: The Moon reflecting heat.
options.why: The Moon is not the reason.

options.text: Air resistance, because the capsule rubs against air at very high speed.

hints: Think about what happens when two things rub together.
The capsule moves very fast through the air.
Which force acts on something moving through air?
items.explanation: The capsule is very fast, so air resistance is very large. This friction turns movement energy into a lot of heat.
